Ezekiel 1: Ezekiel, a priest, is among the exiles "by the river of Chebar" in Babylonia, a canal near Nippur. His call comes in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity (Ezekiel 1:1–3), 593 BC.
Ezekiel 2: God sends Ezekiel to the exiles, "a rebellious nation" (Ezekiel 2:3), and gives him a scroll to eat.
Ezekiel 3: Ezekiel goes to the exiles at Telabib by the river Chebar and sits among them seven days (Ezekiel 3:15).
Ezekiel 4: Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on a clay tile and lies beside it as a sign of the coming siege, which began in 588 BC.
Ezekiel 5: Ezekiel shaves his head and divides the hair in three as a sign of Jerusalem's fate.
Ezekiel 6: Ezekiel prophesies against "the mountains of Israel" (Ezekiel 6:2) and their high places.
Ezekiel 7: "An end is come" (Ezekiel 7:6) on the land of Israel.
Ezekiel 8: In the sixth year, sixth month (Ezekiel 8:1), 592 BC, Ezekiel is carried in a vision to Jerusalem's temple and sees women weeping for Tammuz, a Mesopotamian god.
Ezekiel 9: In the vision, a man with a writer's inkhorn marks those who mourn over Jerusalem's sins before the city is judged.
Ezekiel 10: The glory of the LORD leaves the temple threshold, and Ezekiel recognizes the creatures as the cherubims he saw by the Chebar.
Ezekiel 11: The glory leaves the city and stands on the mountain to the east, the mount of Olives (Ezekiel 11:23).
Ezekiel 12: Ezekiel packs his belongings and digs through a wall as a sign of the king's escape. Zedekiah was captured fleeing Jerusalem in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:4–7).
Ezekiel 13: Ezekiel condemns prophets who say "Peace" when there is no peace (Ezekiel 13:10).
Ezekiel 14: Elders of Israel come to Ezekiel. God names "Noah, Daniel, and Job" as righteous men (Ezekiel 14:14).
Ezekiel 15: Jerusalem is compared to the wood of a vine, useless for making anything.
Ezekiel 16: Jerusalem's history is told as the story of an abandoned baby: "thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite" (Ezekiel 16:3).
Ezekiel 17: A riddle of two eagles describes Babylon taking Jehoiachin and Zedekiah's turn to Egypt for help (Ezekiel 17:12–15).
Ezekiel 18: The exiles quote a proverb: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes" (Ezekiel 18:2), also quoted in Jeremiah 31:29.
Ezekiel 19: A lament for the princes of Israel describes Jehoahaz taken to Egypt and Jehoiachin taken to Babylon.
Ezekiel 20: In the seventh year, fifth month (Ezekiel 20:1), 591 BC, elders come to Ezekiel. He recounts Israel's history from Egypt.
Ezekiel 21: The king of Babylon stands at a fork in the road and divides by arrows, images, and a liver whether to attack Ammon or Jerusalem (Ezekiel 21:21). Babylonian liver models for divination survive.
Ezekiel 22: Jerusalem's sins are listed, and its leaders are compared to dross in a furnace.
Ezekiel 23: Samaria and Jerusalem are pictured as two sisters, Aholah and Aholibah.
Ezekiel 24: On the tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year (Ezekiel 24:1–2), January 588 BC, Babylon begins the siege of Jerusalem. Ezekiel's wife dies that evening.
Ezekiel 25: Oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines begin the oracles against the nations (Ezekiel 25–32).
Ezekiel 26: In the eleventh year (Ezekiel 26:1), 586 BC, Ezekiel prophesies against Tyre. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years.
Ezekiel 27: A lament over Tyre pictures it as a great ship and lists its trading partners from Tarshish to Arabia.
Ezekiel 28: The oracle against the prince of Tyre is followed by one against Sidon.
Ezekiel 29: In the tenth year (Ezekiel 29:1), 587 BC, Ezekiel prophesies against Pharaoh. A later oracle dated to the twenty-seventh year (Ezekiel 29:17), 571 BC, is the latest date in the book.
Ezekiel 30: In the eleventh year (Ezekiel 30:20), Ezekiel says Pharaoh's arm is broken; Pharaoh Hophra had failed to relieve Jerusalem.
Ezekiel 31: In the eleventh year, third month (Ezekiel 31:1), Egypt is compared to Assyria, a great cedar that was cut down. Nineveh fell in 612 BC.
Ezekiel 32: In the twelfth year (Ezekiel 32:1), 585 BC, Ezekiel laments over Pharaoh.
Ezekiel 33: In the twelfth year, tenth month, a refugee arrives in Babylonia saying, "The city is smitten" (Ezekiel 33:21), news that took about five months to arrive.
Ezekiel 34: Ezekiel condemns the shepherds (rulers) of Israel and promises one shepherd, "my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:23).
Ezekiel 35: The oracle against mount Seir (Edom) condemns its joy at Israel's fall.
Ezekiel 36: Ezekiel speaks to "the mountains of Israel" of return, a new heart, and a new spirit.
Ezekiel 37: Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones and joins two sticks for Judah and Joseph.
Ezekiel 38: The prophecy names Gog of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal (Ezekiel 38:2), peoples of Anatolia.
Ezekiel 39: Gog's defeat is followed by seven months of burying the dead (Ezekiel 39:12).
Ezekiel 40: In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell (Ezekiel 40:1), 573 BC, Ezekiel sees a new temple in a vision. Chapters 40–48 describe it.
Ezekiel 41: A man with a measuring reed measures the temple's inner rooms.
Ezekiel 42: The vision continues with the priests' chambers and the outer wall, 500 reeds on each side.
Ezekiel 43: The glory of the LORD returns to the temple from the east (Ezekiel 43:2–4).
Ezekiel 44: The east gate is shut, and only the sons of Zadok may serve as priests at the altar (Ezekiel 44:15).
Ezekiel 45: A holy portion of land is set apart for the temple, priests, and prince.
Ezekiel 46: The chapter gives rules for the prince's offerings and sabbath and new moon worship.
Ezekiel 47: A river flows from the temple to the Dead Sea, making its water fresh from Engedi to Eneglaim (Ezekiel 47:10).
Ezekiel 48: The land is divided among the twelve tribes, and the city is named "The LORD is there" (Ezekiel 48:35).
Daniel 1: In the third year of Jehoiakim (Daniel 1:1), Nebuchadnezzar takes Daniel and other young nobles to Babylon, about 605 BC. Many scholars date the book's final form to the 160s BC; others hold it was written by Daniel in the 6th century BC.
Daniel 2: In Nebuchadnezzar's second year (Daniel 2:1), about 603 BC, the king dreams of a great image. From Daniel 2:4 to 7:28 the book is in Aramaic.
Daniel 3: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.
Daniel 4: Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled 605–562 BC, tells of his dream of a great tree and seven years of madness.
Daniel 5: Belshazzar's feast takes place on the night Babylon falls to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:30–31), October 539 BC.
Daniel 6: Under Darius the Mede, Daniel is thrown into the lions' den. Darius the Mede is not named in other ancient records, and his identity is debated.
Daniel 7: In the first year of Belshazzar (Daniel 7:1), about 553 BC, Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea.
Daniel 8: In Belshazzar's third year, Daniel sees in a vision that he is at Shushan by the river Ulai (Daniel 8:1–2). The book returns to Hebrew.
Daniel 9: In the first year of Darius (Daniel 9:1), about 539 BC, Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years and prays.
Daniel 10: In the third year of Cyrus (Daniel 10:1), about 536 BC, Daniel sees a vision by the Hiddekel (Tigris).
Daniel 11: The vision traces kings of Persia, a mighty king (Alexander, died 323 BC), and wars between the kings of the north and south, matching the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings down to Antiochus IV (175–164 BC).
Daniel 12: The visions close with Michael standing for Daniel's people and Daniel told to "shut up the words, and seal the book" (Daniel 12:4).
